intro: Every martial arts school hangs a sign, and every sign makes a claim. Some claims rest on a teacher's signature on a scroll. Some rest on a numbered certificate from a federation in Tokyo, Seoul or Rio de Janeiro. Others rest on a trademark registered in the United States. In this unit you will follow those claims through real records: a Kyoto society founded in 1895, a karate association that split in 1990 and a Gracie family case decided in 2000.

You will also study the rules that come with a world stage. Olympic fencing, judo, boxing and wrestling changed their gear and scoring to fit the Games. Arts such as Swiss Schwingen, Icelandic glíma and Japanese kendo chose other paths. By the end, you can explain who grants authority in an art, compare an Olympic code with a local one and back your claims with dates and documents.
bigQuestion: Who has the right to say what a martial art is: a founder's line, a federation, a court or a world stage?

timeline.t: Kanō Jigorō gives the first judo dan ranks
The Dai Nippon Butoku Kai is founded in Kyoto; the Swiss wrestling federation is founded
Icelandic wrestlers show glíma at the Stockholm Olympics
Funakoshi Gichin awards the first karate dan ranks
Épée is scored electrically at the Berlin Olympics
The Japan Karate Association is founded in Tokyo
K. D. Jadhav wins India's first individual Olympic medal
The International Kendo Federation is formed
A U.S. appeals court rules in the Gracie trademark case; the blue judogi debuts in Sydney
The IOC votes wrestling back onto the Olympic program
Men box without headgear at the Rio Olympics

words.d: the line of teachers and students through which an art has been passed down
the accepted right to teach, judge or promote others
a license of full transmission in an old Japanese school
a numbered black-belt grade, first used in judo in 1883
a split in a group over who holds authority
an official list, such as a list of every rank a body has granted
a word or symbol, protected by law, that tells buyers who is selling
the ordinary name for a whole kind of thing, which no one can own as a trademark
a body that joins many clubs or schools under shared rules
making gear, sizes or rules the same everywhere
the list of sports and events held at an Olympic Games
a sport shown at an Olympic Games without official medals

test.q: What did a menkyo kaiden record?
choices: A full transmission of an old Japanese school
test.why: It was a license of full transmission given by a teacher.

test.q: Which Kyoto body, founded in 1895, granted teaching titles?
test.why: The Butoku Kai granted titles such as hanshi and kyōshi.

test.q: Who awarded the first karate dan ranks, in 1924?
test.why: Funakoshi gave the first karate dan ranks in Tokyo.

test.q: What happened to the Japan Karate Association in 1990?
test.why: The JKA split in 1990, and the name dispute went to court.

test.q: Where did Maeda Mitsuyo teach Carlos Gracie?
test.why: Maeda settled in Belém and taught Carlos Gracie there.

test.q: What did the Fadda line show?
choices: That lineage can have more than one branch
test.why: Fadda's line runs to Maeda through Luiz França, not the Gracies.

choices: The ordinary name for a whole kind of thing
test.why: Generic words, like karate, cannot be trademarks.

test.q: Where does a federation's control over rank come from?
test.why: A school that never joins can still teach; the federation controls its own events and lists.

test.q: Which fencing weapon was scored electrically first at the Olympics?
test.why: Épée went electric at Berlin in 1936.

test.q: Why was the blue judogi introduced?
choices: So viewers and judges could tell two players apart
test.why: One blue and one white jacket are easy to tell apart on screen.

test.q: When did men first box without headgear at an Olympics since 1980?
test.why: Men boxed without headgear at Rio in 2016.

test.q: What did FILA do after the IOC board moved to drop wrestling in 2013?
choices: It left the Olympics for good
It moved to the World Games
It changed leaders and rules, and won its place back
test.why: The federation reformed and was voted back in September 2013.

test.q: Which sumo code uses weight classes?
choices: Amateur sumo under the International Sumo Federation
test.why: Amateur sumo uses weight classes; professional sumo has one open division.

test.q: What makes Swiss Schwingen's rules different from Olympic wrestling's?
choices: They are written by the IOC
They serve a Swiss festival culture, not a world broadcast
test.why: The Swiss federation answers to its festivals and community.

test.q: Why have kendo leaders in Japan not sought the Olympics?
choices: They argue medals could push the art toward points over character
test.why: Leaders prefer to protect kendo's standard of a valid strike and its aims.

write.prompt: Who should decide what counts in a martial art: a teacher's line, a federation or a world stage? Argue from two or three cases in this unit, such as the JKA split of 1990, the Gracie trademark case of 2000, the blue judogi of 2000 or kendo's non-Olympic path.
tips: Name each record you use and give its date.
Say which institution made each decision and whom it answered to.
Attribute beliefs to the group that holds them, such as kendo leaders in Japan.
Compare two institutions rather than ranking one art above another.
Use unit terms such as lineage, register, trademark and standardization.
